b2014-1.ask: The word KANGAROO is spelled with cards, but some are turned. Each quarter turn is one 90° rotation. How many quarter turns fix all the cards?
steps: Look at each card and ask: how many quarter turns until it looks right?
K needs 2 quarter turns (it's upside down). The first A needs 1.
N is lying on its side (it looks like Z): 1 quarter turn.
The second A is upside down: 2 quarter turns. G, R, O, O are already fine.
b2014-1.check: Go card by card again and make sure you didn't skip any. ✓
b2014-1.spot: Turning shapes? Turn each one in your head a quarter at a time.
b2014-1.oops: Missing the N, which is turned on its side.

b2014-2.ask: A 900 g cake is cut into 4 pieces. The biggest piece weighs as much as the other 3 together. How heavy is the biggest piece?
steps: The biggest piece = the other three together.
So the cake is two equal halves: the biggest piece, and the other three.
Half of 900 g = 450 g.
b2014-2.check: Biggest 450 g, the rest 450 g, total 900 g. ✓
b2014-2.spot: 'One part equals all the others together'? That part is exactly half.
b2014-2.oops: Dividing by 4. The pieces aren't equal.

b2014-3.ask: Peter sees two linked rings from the front. What does Paul see from behind?
steps: From behind, left and right swap, like looking at your reflection the wrong way round.
So the gray ring, which is on one side for Peter, is on the other side for Paul.
Where the rings cross, the part that was in front for Peter is behind for Paul, and the other way round.
Picture D shows both changes.
b2014-3.check: Try it with two rubber bands or bracelets linked together. Look from the front, then from the back. ✓
b2014-3.spot: Seeing from behind? Left and right swap, and front and back swap.
b2014-3.oops: Only swapping sides but forgetting which ring is in front at the crossings.

b2014-4.ask: 1★2 + 1★3 + 1★4 = 309. What do the hidden digits add up to?
steps: Ones column: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9. That's the 9 in 309, with nothing carried.
Hundreds column: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. That's the 3 in 309.
So the tens column must make 0 with nothing carried: ★ + ★ + ★ = 0.
All the stars are 0. Their sum is 0.
b2014-4.spot: Hidden digits? Ones first, then check what each column must make.
b2014-4.oops: Thinking the stars must be something because they're hidden. Zero is a digit too!

b2014-5.ask: What's the smallest 5-digit number minus the largest 4-digit number?
steps: Smallest 5-digit number: 10000.
Largest 4-digit number: 9999.
10000 − 9999 = 1. They're right next to each other!
b2014-5.spot: 'Biggest' and 'smallest' numbers? Write them out first.

b2014-6.ask: A square with perimeter 48 cm is cut in half, and the two halves are put side by side to make a long rectangle. What is the rectangle's perimeter?
steps: Square perimeter 48 cm, so each side is 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm.
Cut in half: two pieces, each 12 cm long and 6 cm wide.
Side by side, end to end: a rectangle 24 cm long and 6 cm tall.
Perimeter: 24 + 6 + 24 + 6 = 60 cm.
b2014-6.check: Same area (144 cm²) ✓, but longer and thinner, so a bigger perimeter. ✓
b2014-6.spot: Shapes rearranged? Write every length on a drawing.
b2014-6.oops: Thinking the perimeter stays 48 because the pieces are the same.

b2014-7.ask: 38 matches make a triangle and a square. Each triangle side is 6 matches. How many matches per square side?
steps: Triangle: 3 sides × 6 = 18 matches.
Left for the square: 38 − 18 = 20 matches.
A square has 4 equal sides: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
b2014-7.spot: A total shared between parts? Take away what you know, then share the rest.

b2014-8.ask: Alex wants 5 dark pearls. She can only take pearls from the ends of the necklace. What's the fewest white pearls she must take?
steps: She can only take pearls from the two ends, so try different mixes of left and right.
Only from the left: to get 5 dark pearls she'd take 4 white. Only from the right: 5 white.
Now mix: take a dark pearl from each end first, then keep taking from whichever end gives dark pearls with the fewest whites in the way.
The best mix takes just 3 white pearls.
b2014-8.check: Look at the necklace and try the best split: you get 5 dark with 3 white. No split does it with 2. ✓
b2014-8.spot: Taking from the ends? Make a neat list of every left-and-right split.

b2014-9.ask: Harry flew 5 laps. The table shows when he passed the start. Which lap was fastest?
steps: Work out each lap: the time from one row to the next.
Lap 5: 12:03 to 12:32 = 29 min. The shortest is lap 2.
b2014-9.spot: Time between clock readings? Count up to the next hour, then add the rest.
b2014-9.oops: Subtracting times like ordinary numbers (10:26 − 9:55 isn't 71 minutes).

b2014-10.ask: On Ben's watch the last digit only shows its up-and-down lines. The time just changed. What time is it now?
steps: You can only see some of the lines of the last digit, so list every digit that could fit.
Before: the lines could belong to 1, 3 or 7, so 12:41, 12:43 or 12:47.
After: the lines could belong to 4 or 9, so 12:44 or 12:49.
The time went up by exactly one minute. Only 12:43 → 12:44 does that.
b2014-10.check: 12:41 → 12:44 is 3 minutes, 12:47 → 12:49 is 2 minutes. Only 3 → 4 is one minute. ✓
b2014-10.spot: Broken displays? Write which lines each digit uses, then match.
b2014-10.oops: Forgetting that the time JUST changed, so the two digits are one minute apart.

b2014-11.ask: Which tile can make the light gray and dark gray areas equal?
steps: Measure everything in whole squares. Two half-squares make one square.
Light gray already adds up to 5 squares. Dark gray adds up to 3 squares.
The missing tile is only 1 square big. Even if it were all dark, dark would only reach 4.
4 is still less than 5. No tile can make them equal.
b2014-11.check: Best case: 3 + 1 = 4 dark against 5 light. Not equal. ✓
b2014-11.spot: Equal areas? Measure everything in small equal pieces, like quarter-tiles.
b2014-11.oops: Picking a tile without counting first.

b2014-12.ask: Henry and John walk from the same point. Which last step brings John to where Henry ended?
steps: Draw both walks on squared paper, 1 square = 1 km.
Henry: up 1, left 2, down 4, left 1. He ends 3 left and 3 down from the start.
John: right 1, down 4, left 4. He ends 3 left and 4 down.
John is 1 km below Henry. He needs to walk 1 km north.
b2014-12.check: 3 left and 4 down, then 1 up = 3 left and 3 down, the same as Henry. ✓
b2014-12.spot: Walks and directions? Draw them on squared paper.
b2014-12.oops: Trying to keep it all in your head and mixing up left and right.

b2014-13.ask: 7 kids eat ice cream every day. 9 kids eat it every other day. Yesterday 13 kids ate ice cream. How many eat it today?
steps: The 7 everyday kids ate yesterday. 13 − 7 = 6 of the every-other-day kids ate yesterday.
Those 6 skip today.
The other 9 − 6 = 3 every-other-day kids eat today.
b2014-13.spot: Groups taking turns? Work out who went yesterday, and the rest go today.

b2014-15.ask: Four of the five pieces make a square. Which one isn't used?
steps: Every piece is a square with curved bits added (bulges) or taken away (dips). Every bulge or dip is the same size.
Count: A has 2 dips, B has none, C has 2 bulges, D has 1 bulge, E has 1 dip.
Four pieces must make a square exactly 4 squares big, so the bulges and dips must cancel out.
Leave out B: 2 bulges + 1 bulge = 3 bulges, 2 dips + 1 dip = 3 dips. They cancel. Leave out anything else and they don't.
b2014-15.check: A, C, D and E fit together with every bulge in a dip. ✓
b2014-15.spot: Fitting pieces? Count bumps and dips: they must match up.
b2014-15.oops: Choosing by how the pieces look instead of checking each curve.

b2014-16.ask: A 3-digit number's digits multiply to 135. What do they add to?
steps: Break 135 into small factors: 135 = 5 × 27 = 5 × 3 × 9.
Each digit must be from 1 to 9. 5, 3 and 9 are all digits.
Other splits don't work (like 1 × 5 × 27, since 27 isn't a digit; or 1 × 15 × 9, since 15 isn't a digit).
b2014-16.spot: Digits that multiply to a number? Break the number into its smallest factors.
b2014-16.oops: Forgetting each digit has to be 9 or less.

b2014-17.ask: 16 tables with 3, 4 or 6 chairs. The 3- and 4-chair tables seat 36. All tables seat 72. How many 3-chair tables?
steps: The 6-chair tables seat 72 − 36 = 36 people: 36 ÷ 6 = 6 tables.
So 16 − 6 = 10 tables have 3 or 4 chairs, seating 36.
If all 10 had 3 chairs: 30. We need 6 more, and each 4-chair table adds 1 more.
So 6 tables have 4 chairs and 4 tables have 3.
b2014-17.spot: Two kinds of things with a total? Pretend they're all the small kind, then count the extras.
b2014-17.oops: Forgetting to work out the 6-chair tables first.

b2014-18.ask: Points A to F are on a line in order. AF = 35, AC = 12, BD = 11, CE = 12, DF = 16. How long is BE?
steps: Draw the line and mark all the lengths.
AC + DF = 12 + 16 = 28. These cover everything except CD. So CD = 35 − 28 = 7.
BD = 11 and CD = 7, so BC = 4. CE = 12 and CD = 7, so DE = 5.
b2014-18.spot: Lengths on a line? Draw it and find the overlapping or missing pieces.
b2014-18.oops: Adding BD + CE and forgetting they overlap.

b2014-19.ask: Marisa's stones leave 2 over in groups of 3 and 2 over in groups of 5. Fewest extra stones so nothing is left over either way?
steps: She has 2 more than a number that fits into both 3s and 5s, so 2 more than a multiple of 15.
For example 17, 32 or 47 stones.
To reach the next multiple of 15, add 15 − 2 = 13.
Then the number divides evenly by 3 and by 5.
b2014-19.spot: Same leftover for different group sizes? Think about numbers that fit both groups.
b2014-19.oops: Adding 1 (to fix groups of 3) or 3 (to fix groups of 5) but not both at once.

b2014-20.ask: Some pairs of cube faces share an edge. Which number is opposite 4?
steps: Face 1 touches 6, 5 and 2. Face 6 touches 1, 5, 4 and 2.
A face touches 4 others and is opposite exactly 1.
6 touches 1, 5, 4, 2, so 6 is opposite 3.
1 touches 6, 5, 2, so 1 is opposite 3 or 4. 3 is taken by 6, so 1 is opposite 4.
b2014-20.check: Opposite pairs: 6–3, 1–4, so 2–5. Every touching pair in the list is allowed. ✓
b2014-20.spot: Faces of a cube? Each face has 4 neighbours and 1 opposite.

b2014-21.ask: How many small cubes do you need to take out of the 3 × 3 × 3 cube so it looks like the picture from the right, from above and from the front?
steps: Look at the picture: from the right and from the front, the top middle square is missing. From above, the front middle is missing.
For the front and right views: take out every top cube in the middle row going front-to-back AND the middle row going side-to-side (they share the centre).
For the top view: take out the whole middle column at the front, all the way down.
Count them without counting any cube twice: 7 cubes.
b2014-21.check: Imagine the cube with those 7 removed. Look from the right, above and front: each matches the picture. ✓
b2014-21.spot: Views of a 3D shape? Check each direction one at a time.

b2014-22.ask: Songs A (3 min), B (2:30), C (2 min), D (1:30), E (4 min) play in a loop. C was playing when Andy left. What's playing one hour later?
steps: One full loop: 3 + 2.5 + 2 + 1.5 + 4 = 13 minutes.
60 minutes = 4 loops (52 min) + 8 minutes.
4 full loops bring us back to the same spot, so we just move 8 minutes ahead.
C plays from 5.5 to 7.5 minutes into a loop. 8 minutes later is 13.5 to 15.5, which is 0.5 to 2.5 minutes into the next loop: song A.
b2014-22.check: A plays from 0 to 3 minutes of each loop, and 0.5 to 2.5 fits inside. ✓
b2014-22.spot: Repeating things? Find the loop length and look at the leftover.
b2014-22.oops: Forgetting that full loops don't change anything.

b2014-23.ask: Numbers 1 to 9 fill a 3 × 3 grid with 1, 3, 2, 4 in the corners. The cells next to 5 add to 9. What do the cells next to 6 add to?
steps: 5 can't be in a corner (the corners are taken). If 5 were in the middle, its 4 neighbours would add to far more than 9. So 5 is on an edge.
An edge cell touches two corners and the centre. Try each edge: only the left edge works, between 1 and 2: 1 + 2 + centre = 9, so the centre is 6.
6 in the centre touches all four edge cells.
The edge cells hold 5 and the leftover numbers 7, 8, 9. 5 + 7 + 8 + 9 = 29.
b2014-23.check: Other edges would need the centre to be 5, 2 or 3, which are already used. ✓
b2014-23.spot: Grid with clues? Start with the cell that has the most limits.
b2014-23.oops: Putting 5 in a spot without checking that the centre number is still free.

b2014-24.ask: 60 trees in a row. Every 2nd tree is a maple. Every 3rd tree is a linden or a maple. The rest are birches. How many birches?
steps: Every 2nd tree is a maple: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 maples.
Every 3rd tree is linden or maple: 60 ÷ 3 = 20 trees.
Some of those 20 are every 6th tree, which are already maples: 60 ÷ 6 = 10. The other 10 are lindens.
Birches: 60 − 30 maples − 10 lindens = 20.
b2014-24.spot: Every 2nd, every 3rd...? Watch out for the ones counted in both (every 6th).
b2014-24.oops: Saying 60 − 30 − 20 = 10, counting the maples on every 6th tree twice.

b2014-25.ask: A ribbon is glued across a see-through cube. Which picture can't be a view of the cube from any side?
steps: Look at the ribbon: on each face it runs as a straight line, joining corners or edges.
Look at the cube from the front, back, sides, top and bottom. Because the cube is clear, you see the ribbon on the near face AND the far face.
Draw what each view shows: some views give an X, some a single diagonal, some just the square.
One of the pictures never appears from any side: E.
b2014-25.check: Each of the other four pictures matches at least one view. ✓
b2014-25.spot: See-through shapes? Remember you see the front and the back at the same time.
b2014-25.oops: Forgetting you can see the far side through the clear plastic.

b2014-26.ask: The king rides at 5 km/h and every hour sends a messenger back to the castle at 10 km/h. How long between messengers arriving?
steps: First messenger: sent after 1 hour, 5 km away. 5 km at 10 km/h takes half an hour. Arrives at 1.5 hours.
Second messenger: sent after 2 hours, 10 km away. Takes 1 hour. Arrives at 3 hours.
Third: sent after 3 hours, 15 km away, takes 1.5 hours. Arrives at 4.5 hours.
Gap each time: 1.5 hours = 90 minutes.
b2014-26.spot: Hard to picture? Work out the first few cases and look for the pattern.
b2014-26.oops: Saying 60 minutes. Each messenger has farther to go than the last.

b2014-27.ask: Three one-digit numbers add to 15. Ali swaps one for a 3, and the three numbers now multiply to 36. Which number could Ali have erased?
steps: After the swap, the numbers are 3 and two numbers that weren't erased. 36 ÷ 3 = 12, so the two kept numbers multiply to 12.
One-digit pairs that multiply to 12: 2 and 6, or 3 and 4.
If they're 2 and 6, the erased number is 15 − 8 = 7.
If they're 3 and 4, the erased number is 15 − 7 = 8. Both work.
b2014-27.spot: More than one answer possible? List every option and check them all.
b2014-27.oops: Finding 7 and stopping without checking for another answer.

b2014-28.ask: Peter eats either 9 carrots, or 2 cabbages, or 1 cabbage + 4 carrots, or only grass each day. In 10 days he ate 30 carrots and 9 cabbages. How many grass days?
steps: Call the mixed days (1 cabbage + 4 carrots) 'mixed'. Carrots come from 9-carrot days and mixed days.
Try numbers of mixed days. 30 − 4 × (mixed) must divide by 9. Mixed = 3 gives 30 − 12 = 18 = 2 × 9. So 2 carrot days.
Cabbages: 3 from mixed days, 9 − 3 = 6 left = 3 cabbage days.
Days used: 2 + 3 + 3 = 8. Grass days: 10 − 8 = 2.
b2014-28.spot: Mixing different kinds of days? Try small numbers for the tricky kind first.
b2014-28.oops: Forgetting the mixed days give both carrots AND a cabbage.

b2014-29.ask: Sunny days always come after 2 rainy days. 5 days after any rainy day it rains again. It's sunny today. How many days ahead can we be sure of the weather?
steps: Today is sunny, so yesterday and the day before were rainy.
Tomorrow: a sunny day needs 2 rainy days before it, but today is sunny. So tomorrow is rainy. Same for the day after: rainy.
5 days after the two rainy days before today: days 3 and 4 from now are rainy.
Day 5: it has 2 rainy days before it, so it could be sunny, but it could also rain. Not certain. So we're sure for 4 days.
b2014-29.check: Days 1, 2, 3, 4 must all be rainy, and day 5 could go either way. ✓
b2014-29.spot: Rules about patterns of days? Go day by day and ask: is this forced?
b2014-29.oops: Thinking you can predict forever. Day 5 has two possibilities.

b2014-30.ask: 10 grandchildren, all different ages, adding to 180. Alice is the oldest. What's the youngest Alice can be?
steps: To keep Alice young, make everyone else as OLD as possible, just under her, all different.
If Alice is A, the oldest the others can be is A − 1, A − 2, ..., A − 9.
Total: 10 × A − (1 + 2 + ... + 9) = 10A − 45. This must reach 180.
10A − 45 ≥ 180 means 10A ≥ 225, so A is at least 22.5. Ages are whole numbers: 23.
b2014-30.check: With A = 22 the most possible is 22 + 21 + ... + 13 = 175, short of 180. With A = 23 it works: 23, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15 and 9 add to 180. ✓
b2014-30.spot: Smallest biggest? Squeeze everyone else as close to the top as allowed.
b2014-30.oops: Dividing 180 by 10 = 18. The ages must all be different.
